Below is a **6‑week, beginner‑friendly strength‑training program** built specifically for a healthy 60‑year‑old who is new to resistance work.  
It balances safety, functional movement, and gradual progression so you can build strength, improve balance, and feel more energetic without over‑loading your joints.

> **Quick safety note** – Before you start, get a brief medical clearance (especially if you have hypertension, heart disease, joint issues, or take medication that affects balance). If any exercise hurts (sharp or “stinging” pain) stop immediately and reassess form or choose a milder option.

---

## 1. How the Program Is Structured

| Day | Focus | Duration | What you’ll do |
|-----|-------|----------|----------------|
| **Mon** | Upper‑body (push‑pull) | 30‑40 min | Full‑body strength circuit (A) |
| **Tue** | Light cardio & mobility | 20‑30 min | Walk, bike, or water‑aerobics + 10 min stretch |
| **Wed** | Lower‑body + core | 30‑40 min | Full‑body strength circuit (B) |
| **Thu** | Active recovery | 20‑30 min | Easy walk, yoga, or tai‑chi |
| **Fri** | Full‑body (lighter) | 30‑40 min | Combined A + B (shorter) |
| **Sat** | Optional fun activity | – | Hiking, swimming, dancing, etc. |
| **Sun** | Rest | – | Complete rest or gentle stroll |

*You can shift the days to match your schedule – just keep at least **one full day of rest** between the two main strength sessions (Mon & Wed).*

### Training Philosophy

| Principle | What it means for you |
|-----------|-----------------------|
| **2‑set, 8‑12 rep range** | Light enough to maintain form, heavy enough to stimulate strength. |
| **Progressive overload** | Every 1‑2 weeks you’ll add a little weight, a rep, or a set. |
| **Whole‑body focus** | You’ll train all major muscle groups each week, which is most efficient for beginners. |
| **Balance & stability** | Core, hip, and ankle work are built into each session to protect joints. |
| **Recovery** | 48‑72 h between heavy sessions, plus mobility work on off‑days. |

---

## 2. Equipment Needed (minimum)

| Item | Why it’s useful | Alternative |
|------|----------------|-------------|
| **Resistance bands** (light & medium) | Ideal for warm‑up, assisted squats, rows, and “new‑to‑weight” work. | Use a sturdy towel for pull‑ups / rows. |
| **Dumbbells** (2‑5 kg each to start) | Most exercises use them. | Filled water bottles, canned food, or a backpack with books. |
| **Chair or sturdy bench** | Support for seated rows, step‑ups, and seated overhead press. | Any stable surface ∼45 cm high. |
| **Exercise mat** | Comfort for floor work. | Carpet or towel. |
| **Optional** – **ankle‑weight cuffs** or **light kettlebell** for added variety. |

---

## 3. Weekly Workout Templates  

Below, “**RPE**” = Rate of Perceived Exertion (0 = nothing, 10 = max). Aim for **RPE 5‑7** on each set (you could do a few more reps, but not a full extra set).  

### **Day A – Upper‑Body (Push‑Pull)**
| # | Exercise | Sets | Reps | Load/Notes |
|---|----------|------|------|------------|
| 1 | **Warm‑up** – Band Pull‑Apart (or arm circles) | 2 | 12‑15 | Light band, focus on shoulder blades together. |
| 2 | **Seated/Standing Dumbbell Chest Press** | 2 | 10‑12 | Press from chest, keep elbows ~45° from torso. |
| 3 | **One‑Arm Dumbbell Row** (support hand on chair) | 2 | 10‑12 each side | Squeeze shoulder blade at the top. |
| 4 | **Standing Dumbbell Shoulder Press** | 2 | 10‑12 | Keep core tight; don’t arch back. |
| 5 | **Biceps Curl** (band or dumbbells) | 2 | 12‑15 | Slow eccentric (lower) phase. |
| 6 | **Triceps Overhead Extension** (single dumbbell) | 2 | 12‑15 | Keep elbows close to ears. |
| 7 | **Core – Standing Wood Chop** (band) | 2 | 8‑10 each side | Slow, controlled rotation. |
| 8 | **Cool‑down** – Gentle shoulder/arm stretch | 1‑2 | 15‑30 s each stretch | |
|**Total Time**|≈30 min|

> **Progression tip:** Add **0.5 kg** to each dumbbell or move to a “medium” band once you can finish **2 sets × 12 reps** with good form on **all** exercises for two consecutive workouts.

---

### **Day B – Lower‑Body + Core**
| # | Exercise | Sets | Reps | Load/Notes |
|---|----------|------|------|------------|
| 1 | **Warm‑up** – March in place + hip circles | 2 | 30 s | |
| 2 | **Sit‑to‑Stand (Chair Squat)** | 2 | 10‑12 | Use the chair for safety; sit back, tap lightly, stand. |
| 3 | **Supported Reverse Lunge** (hand on chair) | 2 | 8‑10 each leg | Keep front knee over ankle. |
| 4 | **Standing Hip Abduction** (band around ankles) | 2 | 12‑15 each side | Hold chair for balance. |
| 5 | **Glute Bridge** | 2 | 12‑15 | Squeeze glutes at top; optional light dumbbell on hips. |
| 6 | **Calf Raise** (holding chair) | 2 | 15‑20 | Slow up & down. |
| 7 | **Core – Bird‑Dog** | 2 | 8‑10 each side | Keep spine neutral. |
| 8 | **Core – Modified Side Plank** (knees down) | 2 | 15‑30 s per side | |
| 9 | **Cool‑down** – Hamstring & quad stretch | 1‑2 | 15‑30 s each | |
|**Total Time**|≈35 min|

> **Progression tip:** When you can perform **2 sets × 15 reps** comfortably, graduate to **weighted** sit‑to‑stand (hold a 2‑kg dumbbell at chest) or add a **light ankle weight** to the hip abduction.

---

### **Day F – Full‑Body “Light” (Optional)**
Use this if you feel good and want extra stimulus. Perform **one set** of each *A* and *B* exercise (choose the easier version of each). Keep the session under 30 min and stop if you feel fatigued.

---

## 4. How to Progress Over 6 Weeks

| Week | Goal | How to Achieve |
|------|------|----------------|
| **1‑2** | Learn solid technique, establish routine | Use the lightest band/dumbbells, focus on full range of motion. |
| **3‑4** | Add a little load or volume | Increase weight by 0.5‑1 kg **or** add a **third set** to the two toughest moves (e.g., rows, squats). |
| **5‑6** | Consolidate strength, start “double‑set” on a few lifts | For 2‑3 exercises, do **3 sets × 8‑12 reps**; keep the rest at 2 sets. |

**Key rule:**  **Never increase more than one variable at a time** (weight, reps, or sets). If you add weight, stay at the same rep range.

### Simple Tracking Sheet (print or copy into a notes app)

| Date | Exercise | Sets x Reps | Weight/Band | RPE | Notes (form, pain, etc.) |
|------|----------|-------------|------------|-----|--------------------------|
| Mon 08/04 | Chest Press | 2×12 | 3 kg each | 6 | Felt good, no shoulder ache |
| Wed 08/06 | Sit‑to‑Stand | 2×12 | Body‑weight | 5 | Slight knee stiffness, added a chair for support |
| … | … | … | … | … | … |

---

## 5. Warm‑Up & Mobility (5‑10 min each session)

| Movement | Duration | Why |
|----------|----------|-----|
| **Arm circles** (forward & backward) | 30 s each | Lubricates shoulder joint |
| **Band pull‑apart** or **scapular wall slides** | 2 × 12 | Activates upper back |
| **March in place + heel‑to‑toe taps** | 1 min | Raises heart rate, primes legs |
| **Hip circles** (standing) | 30 s each direction | Improves hip mobility |
| **Ankle dorsiflexion stretch** (against wall) | 30 s each side | Reduces fall risk |

---

## 6. Cool‑Down & Stretching (5‑7 min)

| Stretch | Hold | Tips |
|---------|------|------|
| Chest doorway stretch | 20‑30 s each side | Keep shoulders down. |
| Cross‑body shoulder stretch | 20‑30 s each side | Gentle pull, no bounce. |
| Standing quad stretch (hold onto chair) | 20‑30 s each side | Knees aligned, hip pulled forward. |
| Seated hamstring stretch | 20‑30 s each side | Keep back straight. |
| Cat‑Cow on all‑ fours | 10 reps | Mobilizes spine. |
| Deep diaphragmatic breathing | 1 min | Returns heart rate to baseline. |

---

## 7. Lifestyle & Nutrition Basics (to support strength)

| Area | Recommendation |
|------|----------------|
| **Protein** | Aim for **1.0 g kg⁻¹ body weight** per day (≈ 60 g for a 60‑kg person). Lean meat, fish, legumes, Greek yogurt, whey or plant‑protein shakes are easy sources. |
| **Hydration** | 1.5‑2 L water daily; more on cardio days. |
| **Sleep** | 7‑8 h quality sleep – essential for muscle repair. |
| **Vitamin D & Calcium** | 800‑1000 IU vitamin D + 1000 mg calcium (food or supplement) to protect bone health. |
| **Gentle cardio** | 2‑3 sessions of 20‑30 min walking, swimming, or stationary bike; keep HR in comfortable “talk‑test” zone. |
| **Joint health** | Omega‑3 rich foods (salmon, flaxseed) or a 1 g EPA/DHA supplement can reduce inflammation. |

---

## 8. Common Questions & Quick Troubleshooting

| Issue | Quick Fix |
|-------|-----------|
| **My knees hurt during squats** | Reduce depth, sit back onto a higher chair, or replace with **wall sit** (30 s). |
| **Shoulder feels tight** | Add extra scapular‑retraction warm‑up (band rows) and avoid heavy overhead press until mobility improves. |
| **I can’t finish the reps** | Drop the weight or use a band for assistance; finish the set with a **partial range** (e.g., only go halfway down). |
| **I’m sore >48 h** | Make sure you’re stretching, hydrating, and getting >7 h sleep. Consider a light walk or gentle yoga on the sore day. |
| **I want variety after 6 weeks** | Switch to **circuit style** (move from one exercise to the next with minimal rest) or add a new tool (kettlebell swings, seated leg press, resistance‑tube chest fly). |

---

## 9. Example 6‑Week Calendar (fill‑in)

```
Mon 08/04 – A
Tue 08/05 – Light cardio + mobility
Wed 08/06 – B
Thu 08/07 – Active recovery (yoga/tai‑chi)
Fri 08/08 – Light full‑body (optional)
Sat 08/09 – Fun activity (walk, swim)
Sun 08/10 – Rest
```

*(Repeat the same pattern for the next 5 weeks, applying the progression rules above.)*

---

### Final Thought

Strength training at 60 is a fantastic way to preserve muscle mass, support bone density, improve balance, and stay independent. Stick with the plan for at least **8‑12 weeks** and you’ll notice:

* Easier getting up from chairs & stairs  
* Less “creaky” feeling in shoulders & knees  
* More confidence in everyday tasks (grocery bags, gardening, playing with grandchildren)

Enjoy the journey, listen to your body, and celebrate every small win! 🎉

**If you have any specific constraints (e.g., a knee brace, limited equipment, or a health condition) let me know and I can tweak the program further.** Good luck!

#### Highlights of the Riverstone Ridge Trail  
- **Length & Difficulty:** 4.2 mi, moderate grade – suitable for both seasoned hikers and families with active children.  
- **Scenic Features:** Elevated ridge viewpoints, a restored 19th‑century stone bridge over Pinebrook Creek, and an interpretive boardwalk through a rare riparian meadow.

“**Riverstone Ridge Trail is a testament to our commitment to expanding outdoor recreation while preserving the natural beauty of Pinebrook**,” said **Rebecca Alvarez**, Director of State Parks & Recreation. “We’ve worked closely with community volunteers, indigenous groups, and conservation scientists to create a trail that educates, inspires, and safeguards the landscape for generations to come.”

#### Community Involvement  
The project was a collaborative effort involving:

- **Friends of Pinebrook** – over 150 volunteers contributed 2,800 hours of labor for trail clearing, signage installation, and habitat planting.

All events are free and open to the public.  

#### About Pinebrook State Park  
Established in 1938, Pinebrook State Park spans 5,600 acres of woodlands, wetlands, and rolling hills in the heart of [State]. The park offers camping, kayaking, wildlife viewing, and a network of over 20 miles of multi‑use trails. Its mission is to provide **accessible, educational, and sustainable outdoor experiences** while protecting the region’s natural and cultural resources.

#### Media Information  
High‑resolution photos, trail maps, and interview opportunities with park officials are available upon request.

## Podcast Episode Outline  
**Title:** *“The Vanishing Masterpieces: Inside the Isabella Stewart Gardner Heist”*  
**Series:** *Crime & Canvas* – Episode 4  
**Run‑time:** ~45 minutes  

---

### 1. **Teaser (0:00‑0:45)**
- **Audio Cue:** Night‑time street sounds → police radio chatter → a faint glass shatter.  
- **Host (V.O.):** “One night in March 1990, twelve priceless works vanished from a Boston museum. Thirty‑five years later, they’re still missing. This is the story of the greatest art heist in history… and the hunt that still haunts the art world.”  
- Quick montage of interview sound bites (detective, art historian, former thief) ending with a cliff‑hanger: “I’m pretty sure the paintings are still out there.”

### 2. **Opening Credits & Sponsor (0:45‑2:00)**
- **Music:** Dark, minimalist strings.  
- **Credits:** Host, producer, sound designer, research assistants.  
- **Sponsor Spot (30 sec).**

### 3. **Setting the Stage (2:00‑7:00)**
| Segment | Content |
|---------|---------|
| **3.1. The Museum** | Brief history of the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum; description of the sumptuous Venetian‑style courtyard and its “gallery of paintings”. |
| **3.2. The Loot** | Overview of the twelve works stolen: Vermeer’s *The Concert*, Rembrandt’s *The Storm on the Sea of Galilee*, Degas, Manet, and five others. Include images (refer to podcast website). |
| **3.3. Cultural Value** | Why these pieces matter: rarity, market value (>$500 M today), and their place in American art‑collecting history. |
| **3.4. The Night of March 18, 1990** | Timeline of events leading up to the heist: the museum’s security routine, the “after‑hours” staff, the broken elevator, a missing night‑shift guard. |

### 4. **The Heist Unfolds (7:00‑15:00)**
| Segment | Content |
|---------|---------|
| **4.1. The Intruders** | Description of the two men in plain clothes, their use of a police‑style badge, and how they subdued the security guard. |
| **4.2. The Inside Job Theory** | Evidence that points to insider knowledge (elevator key, familiarity with guard schedules). |
| **4.3. The Execution** | Step‑by‑step reenactment (scripted, voice‑acted) of the thieves’ movements through the galleries, the loading of paintings into a stolen Lincoln Town Car. |
| **4.4. Immediate Aftermath** | The guard’s call to police, the discovery of the emptied frames, and the museum’s shock. |
| **Audio Insert:** Police dispatch transcript (real audio, if available). |

### 5. **Investigation & Early Leads (15:00‑23:00)**
| Segment | Content |
|---------|---------|
| **5.1. The FBI’s Art Crime Team** | Formation of the task force; introduction of lead investigator (e.g., Special Agent Robert K. “Bobby” O’Malley). |
| **5.2. First Suspects** | The “Cousin” theory (Giacomo “Jack” Falcone), connections to the Boston underworld, and why the case went cold. |
| **5.3. Provenance Checks** | How experts tracked any attempt to sell or exhibit the missing works; the role of the Art Loss Register. |
| **5.4. Lost Leads** | The “hand‑cuffed” painting found in 1991 (the stolen frame of *The Concert*) – dead‑end but a tantalizing clue. |
| **Interview Clip:** Art historian on why Vermeer’s *The Concert* is a “once‑in‑a‑lifetime” loss. |

### 6. **The Mystery Deepens (23:00‑30:00)**
| Segment | Content |
|---------|---------|
| **6.1. Organized Crime Links** | The involvement of the New England Mafia, the “Boston Black Mass” syndicate, and the possible role of the “Bermuda Triangle” smuggling route. |
| **6.2. The 2013 FBI “Sting”** | Description of the operation that led to the seizure of a stolen *Degas* and *Manet* in a Florida storage unit – later proved unrelated. |
| **6.3. The “Ransom” Offer** | 1994 anonymous tip offering $10 M for the return of the works; why the FBI declined. |
| **6.4. Recent Revelations** | 2022 NYPD cooperation with Italian Carabinieri; a sealed indictment against a former Boston mobster (name withheld). |
| **Interview Clip:** Former FBI art‑crime specialist on why the case remains “cold but not dead.” |

### 7. **Impact & Cultural Legacy (30:00‑37:00)**
| Segment | Content |
|---------|---------|
| **7.1. Museum’s Response** | Restoration of the empty frames, the “empty gallery” exhibit, and the symbolic $10 M reward offered by the museum (still standing). |
| **7.2. Pop‑Culture Footprint** | References in *The Thomas Crown Affair*, *Ocean’s Twelve*, and countless documentaries; how the heist shaped security protocols worldwide. |
| **7.3. Ethical Debate** | The moral quandary of paying ransom for stolen art vs. preserving the integrity of the market. |
| **Listener Quote:** Social media reaction from a Boston resident who witnessed the police arrival in 1990. |

### 8. **Current Status & Theories (37:00‑42:00)**
| Segment | Content |
|---------|---------|
| **8.1. Where Are They?** | Summary of the most credible theories: hidden in a private collection, melted down, or stored in a New York warehouse. |
| **8.2. New Technology** | Use of AI image‑recognition, blockchain provenance tracking, and forensic pigment analysis to locate the works. |
| **8.3. “If We Find Them”** | What would happen legally (repatriation, insurance payouts, criminal charges). |
| **Interview Clip:** Independent art‑recovery lawyer on the legal process of reclaiming stolen works. |

### 9. **Conclusion & Call to Action (42:00‑44:30)**
- **Host Recap:** Key takeaways—why the Gardner heist still resonates, the unsolved mystery’s power to fuel both crime‑fighting and imagination.
- **Public Appeal:** Reminder of the $10 M reward, instructions for tip submission (website, phone line, encrypted email).  
- **Teaser for Next Episode:** “Next week we’ll dive into the 2009 Louvre heist—when a thief walked out with a priceless Matisse and vanished into the night.”

### 10. **Credits & End Music (44:30‑45:00)**
- Full production credits, thank‑you to interviewees, archival archives, and legal disclaimer.  
- Closing music fades out (slow piano with distant siren echo).

## Production Notes
- **Research Sources:** FBI case files (FOIA), museum archives, court transcripts, *The Gardner Heist* documentary (2015), books by Robert Durden & Thomas Hoving.  
- **Audio Assets:** Museum ambient sound, police radio logs, reenactment voice‑overs, interview recordings (remote via Zencastr), archival news clips (WBZ, 1990).  
- **Visual Companion:** Episode webpage featuring high‑resolution images of each missing work, timeline infographic, and interactive map of alleged sightings.  
- **Legal Clearance:** Verify all quoted material; ensure use of copyrighted images falls under fair‑use for commentary.  

---

**Result:** A tightly‑structured, 45‑minute episode that blends narrative storytelling, expert insight, and immersive sound design—perfect for true‑crime fans and art lovers alike.

|21| “If a coworker is out sick and you’re asked to cover a portion of their duties, how would you handle it?” | Flexibility and willingness to pitch‑in. |
|22| “Do you have any questions about our company culture, expectations, or the day‑to‑day of this role?” | Their curiosity and seriousness about fit. |

## 6. Closing & Administrative  

| # | Question | What you’re looking for |

|24| “When would you be able to start, should you be selected?” | Timeline for onboarding. |
|25| “Do you have any certifications (e.g., CPR, first‑aid, Office Management) or training that you think are relevant?” | Additional qualifications. |

---

### How to Use This List  

1. **Start with the warm‑up questions** to put the candidate at ease and get a quick overview of their background.  
2. **Mix skill‑focused and behavioral questions** throughout the interview rather than clustering them; this keeps the conversation natural.  
3. **Take notes using the STAR framework** (Situation, Task, Action, Result) for each behavioral answer—helps compare candidates objectively.  
4. **Score each response** on a brief rubric (e.g., 1–5) for communication, problem‑solving, and cultural fit, then total the scores for a quick comparative view.  
5. **Wrap up with the candidate’s own questions**—their curiosity often reveals what they value most (e.g., growth, work‑life balance, team dynamics).

Below is a ready‑to‑use question bank you can copy‑paste into your interview scorecard.  
Feel free to cherry‑pick, combine, or adapt them to the level (Junior / Mid‑level / Senior) and the specific domain (Web, Mobile, API, Embedded, etc.) of the tester you’re hiring.

---

## 1️⃣  Foundations & Theory  

| # | Question | What you’re looking for |
|---|----------|------------------------|
| F1 | **What is the difference between verification and validation?** | Understanding of V‑&‑V concepts and ability to articulate them. |
| F2 | **Explain the five testing levels (unit, integration, system, acceptance, regression).** | Knowledge of the testing pyramid and when each level applies. |
| F3 | **What are the main test design techniques you use and why?** (e.g., boundary value, equivalence partitioning, decision tables, state‑transition, pairwise) | Ability to choose the right technique for the problem. |
| F4 | **What is a test case? What are its essential components?** | Awareness of good test case structure (ID, pre‑conditions, steps, expected result, post‑conditions, data). |
| F5 | **Define “defect lifecycle” (or bug lifecycle) and walk me through each stage.** | Familiarity with the tracking process (New → Open → Assigned → Fixed → Verified → Closed / Reopened, etc.). |
| F6 | **What is the difference between static and dynamic testing?** | Recognizes reviews, walkthroughs, static analysis vs. execution‑based testing. |
| F7 | **What is a “test plan” and what does it normally contain?** | Understanding of documentation and scope, resources, schedule, risks, entry/exit criteria. |

---

## 2️⃣  Manual Testing / Exploratory Skills  

| # | Question | What you’re looking for |
|---|----------|------------------------|
| M1 | **Describe your most recent exploratory testing session. How did you decide what to test?** | Ability to think on‑the‑fly, use heuristics, and capture findings. |
| M2 | **How do you prioritize test cases when time is limited?** | Use of risk‑based testing, business impact, defect density, critical path. |
| M3 | **What techniques do you use for writing effective bug reports?** | Clear titles, steps to reproduce, severity vs. priority, screenshots/logs, expected vs. actual. |
| M4 | **Give an example of a missed defect that later caused a big problem. What would you have done differently?** | Learning from mistakes, process improvement mindset. |
| M5 | **How do you handle flaky or non‑deterministic tests (manual or automated)?** | Investigation steps, environment stability, test data isolation. |
| M6 | **Walk me through a test case you wrote for a complex UI flow (e.g., multi‑step wizard).** | Ability to capture pre‑conditions, data dependencies, state management. |

---

## 3️⃣  Automation – Concepts & Hands‑On  

| # | Question | What you’re looking for |
|---|----------|------------------------|
| A1 | **What parts of testing do you think should be automated first? Why?** | Understanding of ROI, regression hot‑spots, data‑driven tests, stable UI. |
| A2 | **Which automation frameworks have you used (Selenium, Cypress, Playwright, Appium, RestAssured, etc.)? Describe the architecture of a framework you built.** | Depth of experience, modular design (Page‑Object, Service‑Object, data‑driven, keyword‑driven). |
| A3 | **Explain the difference between a “hard” assertion and a “soft” assertion. When would you use each?** | Knowledge of test flow control and reporting. |
| A4 | **How do you manage test data in automated tests?** | Techniques: fixtures, factories, CSV/JSON, test‑data generators, database seeding, mocking. |
| A5 | **What is CI/CD and how do you integrate automated tests into a pipeline?** | Experience with Jenkins, GitLab CI, Azure DevOps, GitHub Actions, build triggers, test reports, gating. |
| A6 | **Describe a situation where you had to debug a failing automated test. What steps did you take?** | Systematic troubleshooting (logs, screenshots, re‑run locally, environment comparison). |
| A7 | **Performance / load testing – have you ever used JMeter, Gatling, Locust, k6, etc.? Tell us about the test scenario you created and the metrics you monitored.** | For teams that need non‑functional testing knowledge. |
| A8 | **Security testing basics – have you ever written a script to test for OWASP Top‑10 issues?** | Shows awareness of security testing foundations. |

---

## 4️⃣  API / Backend Testing  

| # | Question | What you’re looking for |
|---|----------|------------------------|
| API1 | **How do you test a RESTful API? Which tools have you used?** | Use of Postman, Insomnia, RestAssured, SoapUI, curl, HTTPie. |
| API2 | **What are the key components of an HTTP request/response you validate?** | Status code, headers, body schema, response time, authentication, pagination. |
| API3 | **Explain how you would test an endpoint that handles file uploads.** | Multipart/form‑data, size limits, virus scan simulation, invalid file types. |
| API4 | **Describe a situation where you used contract testing (e.g., Pact, OpenAPI validation).** | Ensuring consumer‑provider compatibility. |
| API5 | **How do you handle test environments that require dynamic data (e.g., IDs generated on the fly)?** | Capture responses, use them in subsequent calls, cleanup, data seeding. |

---

## 5️⃣  Non‑Functional Testing  

| # | Question | What you’re looking for |
|---|----------|------------------------|
| NF1 | **What is the difference between load, stress, and soak testing?** | Understanding of performance test types. |
| NF2 | **How do you measure and evaluate usability?** | Heuristic evaluation, user‑testing, eye‑tracking, surveys, metrics (task success rate, time on task). |
| NF3 | **Explain the concept of “test coverage”. How do you measure it for functional and non‑functional tests?** | Code coverage tools, requirement traceability matrix, risk coverage. |
| NF4 | **What is a Service Level Agreement (SLA) and how would you verify it?** | Response time, uptime, error rate – monitoring tools and alerting. |

---

## 6️⃣  Agile / DevOps Practices  

| # | Question | What you’re looking for |
|---|----------|------------------------|
| Ag1 | **How do you collaborate with developers, product owners, and designers in a Scrum team?** | Transparency, daily stand‑ups, participation in backlog grooming, sprint demos. |
| Ag2 | **What is “Shift‑Left” testing and why is it valuable?** | Early testing, unit‑level validation, static analysis, collaboration. |
| Ag3 | **How do you handle a situation where a defect is classified as “won’t fix” by the product owner?** | Negotiation, risk assessment, documentation, escalation process. |
| Ag4 | **Explain the “Definition of Done” (DoD) for testing.** | Acceptance criteria, regression coverage, documentation, test automation passed, performance benchmarks. |
| Ag5 | **Describe how you use a “Test‑Driven Development (TDD)” or “Behavior‑Driven Development (BDD)” workflow.** | Writing failing tests first, using Cucumber/Gherkin, collaboration on acceptance criteria. |

---

## 7️⃣  Problem‑Solving / Scenario‑Based  

| # | Question | What you’re looking for |
|---|----------|------------------------|
| S1 | **You discover a flaky test that fails intermittently in CI but passes locally. Walk me through your investigation.** | Root‑cause analysis: environment differences, timing issues, shared resources, data pollution. |
| S2 | **Your test suite is taking 3 hours to run, and you need to cut it down to under 30 minutes for each commit. What steps would you take?** | Parallel execution, test selection, hardware scaling, test data caching, test suite refactor. |
| S3 | **A critical bug is found in production after release. How do you respond?** | Immediate triage, rollback decision, hot‑fix process, post‑mortem, preventive actions. |
| S4 | **Your team wants to adopt a new test automation tool. How would you evaluate it?** | Criteria: learning curve, language support, integration with CI/CD, community, licensing, maintainability. |
| S5 | **Explain how you would test a feature that must work across multiple browsers, devices, and OS versions.** | Cross‑browser testing strategy, use of device labs (BrowserStack, Sauce Labs), test matrix, prioritization. |

---

## 8️⃣  Behavioral / Culture Fit  

| # | Question | What you’re looking for |
|---|----------|------------------------|
| B1 | **Tell me about a time you disagreed with a developer about a defect’s severity. How did you handle it?** | Communication, empathy, data‑driven argument, conflict resolution. |
| B2 | **Describe a situation where you had to learn a new tool or technology quickly. What was your approach?** | Self‑learning, resources, mentorship, applying knowledge. |
| B3 | **How do you stay current with testing trends and emerging technologies?** | Blogs, conferences, certifications, community contributions. |
| B4 | **Give an example of a process improvement you championed in a previous team. What impact did it have?** | Initiative, measurable outcomes (e.g., defect leakage reduction, cycle‑time improvement). |
| B5 | **What motivates you as a tester?** | Passion for quality, curiosity, user empathy, problem solving. |

---

### How to Use This List

1. **Pick a core set** (5–7 questions) for each interview stage (phone screen, technical deep‑dive, culture fit).  
2. **Mix levels** – include at least one junior‑level question and one senior‑level question to gauge depth.  
3. **Add live tasks** (e.g., “Write a simple Selenium script to login to a demo site” or “Create a small Postman collection for a CRUD API”).  
4. **Score consistently** – assign a 1‑5 rating per answer and capture notes on evidence of skill/experience.  

Feel free to edit, combine, or reorder to suit your hiring workflow. Good luck with the interview process! 🚀

Below is a ready‑to‑use **behavioral‑interview guide** you can hand to the hiring team (or paste into your interview scorecard) by Friday.  
It’s broken into three parts:

1. **How to use the list** – a quick “starter‑kit” for you and the interviewers.  
2. **Core competency blocks** – the skills a sales associate should demonstrate.  
3. **Behavioral questions** – 4‑6 STAR‑style prompts per competency (plus optional follow‑ups).

Feel free to copy‑paste, edit, or reorder the questions to match the specifics of your organization.

---

## 1️⃣ Quick‑Start: Using the Guide

| Step | What to Do | Why It Matters |
|------|------------|----------------|
| **a. Choose 4–5 competencies** | Scan the list below and pick the ones that matter most for the role (e.g., “Closing Deals,” “Customer‑Centric Problem Solving”). | Keeps the interview focused and avoids fatigue. |
| **b. Pick 2–3 questions per competency** | Choose the strongest prompts (or the ones you haven’t asked before). | Provides enough data points for a reliable assessment. |
| **c. Build a scorecard** | For each question, rate the candidate on the **STAR** (Situation, Task, Action, Result) elements on a 1‑5 scale, plus a “red‑flag” column for disqualifying behaviors. | Turns narrative answers into objective data. |
| **d. Share in advance** | Send the competency list & sample questions to interviewers 24 hrs before the interview. | Gives interviewers time to think of probing follow‑ups. |
| **e. Debrief** | After the interview, each interviewer fills out the scorecard and a brief “overall impression” note. Consolidate scores in a shared Google Sheet or ATS. | Enables a fast, evidence‑based decision before Friday. |

---

## 2️⃣ Core Competency Blocks for a Sales Associate

| Competency | What It Looks Like on the Job | Typical Red Flags |
|------------|------------------------------|-------------------|
| **1. Prospecting & Lead Generation** | Consistently identifies, qualifies, and builds pipelines. | “I never really plan my outreach.” |
| **2. Relationship Building & Customer Service** | Turns first‑time buyers into repeat customers; anticipates needs. | “I only care about the sale, not the client.” |
| **3. Consultative Selling & Needs‑Based Solutioning** | Asks probing questions, matches product benefits to pain points. | “I push the same script on everyone.” |
| **4. Closing & Negotiation** | Moves prospects to purchase, handles objections, creates win‑win deals. | “I get nervous when the price is discussed.” |
| **5. Goal Orientation & Results Tracking** | Sets measurable targets, monitors KPIs, adjusts tactics. | “I rarely track my numbers.” |
| **6. Team Collaboration & Knowledge Sharing** | Shares best practices, mentors junior reps, works cross‑functionally. | “I work in isolation.” |
| **7. Adaptability & Learning Agility** | Thrives in changing market conditions, adopts new tools (CRM, digital selling). | “I resist new processes.” |
| **8. Ethical Conduct & Compliance** | Follows company policy, discloses conflicts, respects data privacy. | “I’d bend the rules to close a deal.” |

*(You can pick any 4–5 of these; the list is exhaustive to give you flexibility.)*

---

## 3️⃣ Behavioral Interview Questions (STAR Format)

### 1. Prospecting & Lead Generation
1. **Tell me about a time you built a pipeline from scratch.**  
   *Probe:* How did you identify prospects? What tools did you use? What was the outcome?
2. **Describe a situation where your usual prospecting method stopped working.**  
   *Probe:* What did you change? How quickly did you see results?
3. **Give an example of a time you exceeded a lead‑generation quota.**  
   *Probe:* What specific actions drove the over‑achievement?

### 2. Relationship Building & Customer Service
1. **Walk me through a case where you turned an unhappy customer into a loyal advocate.**  
   *Probe:* What steps did you take to understand the issue? How did you follow‑up?
2. **Share an example of how you cultivated a long‑term relationship with a key account.**  
   *Probe:* What routine activities kept the relationship alive?
3. **Tell me about a time you discovered an unmet need for a client and acted on it.**  
   *Probe:* How did you surface the need, and what solution did you propose?

### 3. Consultative Selling & Needs‑Based Solutioning
1. **Describe a sale where you had to ask a series of diagnostic questions before proposing a solution.**  
   *Probe:* What questions did you ask? How did the answer shape your pitch?
2. **Give an example of a time you matched a product feature to a customer’s hidden pain point.**  
   *Probe:* How did you uncover the hidden pain? What was the result?
3. **Tell me about a situation where you had to tailor a standard offering to fit a unique customer scenario.**  
   *Probe:* Who was involved in customizing the solution?

### 4. Closing & Negotiation
1. **Share a story of a high‑stakes negotiation that you successfully closed.**  
   *Probe:* What were the main objections? How did you address them?
2. **Describe a time you lost a deal and what you learned.**  
   *Probe:* Which part of the process could you have improved?
3. **Tell me about a time you used a creative concession to seal a sale.**  
   *Probe:* How did you ensure it was a win‑win?

### 5. Goal Orientation & Results Tracking
1. **Give an example of a quarterly sales target you set for yourself and how you achieved it.**  
   *Probe:* What metrics did you track daily/weekly?
2. **Describe a time you missed a quota. What corrective actions did you take?**  
   *Probe:* How quickly did you implement the changes?
3. **Tell me about a time you used data/analytics to improve your sales performance.**  
   *Probe:* Which data points mattered most?

### 6. Team Collaboration & Knowledge Sharing
1. **Share a story of when you helped a teammate close a difficult deal.**  
   *Probe:* What specific assistance did you provide?
2. **Describe a time you introduced a new sales tactic or tool to your team.**  
   *Probe:* How did you gain buy‑in? What impact did it have?
3. **Tell me about a cross‑functional project you participated in (e.g., marketing, product).**  
   *Probe:* How did you align sales goals with other functions?

### 7. Adaptability & Learning Agility
1. **Tell me about a major market or product change you had to adapt to quickly.**  
   *Probe:* What steps did you take to stay effective?
2. **Give an example of when you learned a new technology (CRM, sales automation) and applied it.**  
   *Probe:* What was the learning curve and payoff?
3. **Describe a time you received unexpected feedback and how you acted on it.**  

### 8. Ethical Conduct & Compliance
1. **Share an instance where you faced an ethical dilemma in a sales situation.**  
   *Probe:* What was the decision process, and what was the outcome?
2. **Tell me about a time you discovered a compliance breach (e.g., pricing, data privacy) and what you did.**  
   *Probe:* How did you report it and prevent recurrence?

---

## 4️⃣ Sample Scorecard (One Row per Question)

| Candidate | Competency | Question | Situation (1‑5) | Task (1‑5) | Action (1‑5) | Result (1‑5) | Red‑Flag? (Y/N) | Overall Rating (Avg.) |
|-----------|------------|----------|-----------------|-----------|--------------|--------------|-----------------|-----------------------|
| Jane Doe  | Closing    | #1 (Negotiation) | 4 | 5 | 4 | 5 | N | 4.5 |
| …         | …          | …        | …               | …         | …            | …            | …               | …                     |

*Tip:* Add a **“Notes”** column for any particularly compelling (or concerning) details the interviewers want to capture.

---

### ✅ Quick “Copy‑Paste” Email to Your Manager (Optional)

> **Subject:** Behavioral‑Interview Toolkit for Sales Associate – Ready for Friday  
> **Body:**  
> Hi [Manager’s Name],  
> I’ve put together a reusable interview guide (see attached) that includes:
> 1. A short “how‑to” for interviewers.  
> 2. Core sales‑associate competencies.  
> 3. 2‑4 STAR‑style questions per competency, plus probing follow‑ups.  
> 4. A ready‑to‑use scorecard template.  
> Please let me know if you’d like any tweaks (e.g., specific product‑knowledge focus). I can have the final version uploaded to the ATS by EOD Thursday.  
> Thanks,  
> [Your Name]

---

### What to Do Next (by Friday)

| Day | Action |
|-----|--------|
| **Mon‑Tue** | Review the competency list with the hiring lead; pick the top 4–5. |
| **Tue** | Select 2–3 questions per chosen competency; copy them into the shared interview guide. |
| **Wed** | Build the scorecard (Google Sheet or ATS custom field). |
| **Thu** | Distribute the guide & scorecard to all interviewers; run a 15‑min “STAR‑question practice” call. |
| **Fri** | Conduct interviews, collect scores, and send a brief recommendation to the hiring manager. |

---

**That’s it!** You now have a complete, ready‑to‑use set of behavioral interview questions plus a simple workflow to get the hiring team aligned before Friday. Good luck, and feel free to ask if you need any tweaks for your specific product line or sales model. 🚀

Below is a ready‑to‑use list of interview questions (with optional probing follow‑ups) that covers the most critical areas you’ll want to explore when hiring a **Head Chef**. ## 1️⃣ Culinary Expertise & Vision

| 3 | **Describe a time you had to adapt a menu for a dietary restriction (e.g., gluten‑free, vegan, allergen‑free) while maintaining quality.** | Checks flexibility and knowledge of alternative ingredients. |
| 4 | **What is your philosophy on plating and presentation, and how do you ensure consistency across the team?** | Reveals aesthetic standards and training methods. |
| 5 | **Tell us about a dish or technique you’ve never mastered but are actively learning.** | Shows humility, growth mindset, and willingness to keep learning. |

---

## 2️⃣ Leadership & Team Management  

| # | Question | Why It Matters / Follow‑up Prompts |
|---|----------|------------------------------------|
| 6 | **How do you structure a typical kitchen brigade for a service of X covers?** | Assesses organizational ability. Follow‑up: “How would you adjust for a sudden 30% surge?” |
| 7 | **Describe a situation where you had to address a performance issue with a line cook. What steps did you take, and what was the outcome?** | Tests conflict resolution and coaching style. |

| 9 | **How do you foster a culture of continuous improvement and feedback in the kitchen?** | Checks for systematic training and communication. |
|10 | **Can you give an example of a time you promoted from within? What qualities did you prioritize?** | Shows commitment to career pathways. |

---

## 3️⃣ Operations & Efficiency  

| # | Question | Why It Matters / Follow‑up Prompts |
|---|----------|------------------------------------|
|11| **Walk us through your typical pre‑service routine (mise en place, equipment checks, staff briefing, etc.).** | Reveals preparation rigor and checklist habits. |
|12| **What strategies have you implemented to reduce waste and improve yield without compromising quality?** | Demonstrates cost‑consciousness and sustainability. |
|13| **How do you handle a sudden equipment failure (e.g., oven out) during service?** | Tests problem‑solving under pressure. |
|14| **Describe your experience managing inventory and ordering. Which software or systems have you used?** | Checks technical proficiency and budgeting skills. |
|15| **How do you balance the need for speed during peak service with the demand for meticulous plating?** | Looks for workflow optimization. |

## 4️⃣ Financial Acumen

## 5️⃣ Food Safety & Compliance  

| # | Question | Why It Matters / Follow‑up Prompts |
|---|----------|------------------------------------|
|21| **What are the most critical food‑safety protocols you enforce daily, and how do you ensure the team follows them?** | Looks for knowledge of HACCP, temperature controls, etc. |
|22| **Describe a time you identified a potential safety violation and what you did to correct it.** | Tests vigilance and corrective action. |

## 6️⃣ Creativity, Innovation & Brand Fit

## 7️⃣ Personal Fit & Soft Skills  

| # | Question | Why It Matters / Follow‑up Prompts |

|31| **What motivated you to become a chef, and why do you want this head‑chef role specifically?** | Looks for passion and alignment with the opportunity. |

|34| **Tell us about a time you had to make a quick decision that went against the “standard procedure.” What happened?** | Tests judgment and accountability. |
|35| **Outside of the kitchen, what interests or activities keep you balanced?** | Gives insight into work‑life balance and cultural fit. |

---

### How to Use This List

1. **Prioritize** – Choose 8‑12 questions that align with the most critical competencies for your operation.
2. **Structure** – Start with vision/creative questions, move into operational/leadership, then wrap up with cultural fit.
3. **Score** – Create a simple rating rubric (e.g., 1‑5) for each answer and note any red‑flag or standout moments.
4. **Probe** – Use the follow‑up prompts to dig deeper when a candidate’s answer is vague or particularly interesting.

**Celebrating 30 Years of Teaching – A Retirement Speech for Mrs. Evelyn Carter**

*(Adjust the name, title, and any personal details to fit your beloved retiree.)*  

---

Good afternoon, friends, family, colleagues, and, most importantly, our guest of honor—Mrs. Evelyn Carter.

It is both a privilege and a little bit of a heartbreak to stand before you today. Today we are here to celebrate a milestone that many of us can only imagine: thirty remarkable years of shaping minds, touching hearts, and building a community—one lesson plan, one hallway conversation, and one gentle smile at a time.

---

### 1. A Journey That Began With a Dream  

Thirty years ago, Evelyn walked into our school carrying a briefcase full of freshly printed worksheets, a stack of textbooks, and an even larger stack of dreams. Fresh from the university, she told us that she wanted to be “the kind of teacher who makes learning feel like an adventure.” Little did we know that the adventure she’d create would stretch far beyond the walls of any classroom.

---

### 2. What She Has Given Us  

**A. The Classroom as a Second Home**  
When you entered Mrs. Carter’s room, it felt less like a place to sit at desks and more like stepping into a welcoming living room. Posters of poetry, constellations, and historic photographs weren’t just decoration—they were invitations to explore. Every Friday, the “Mystery Box” challenge turned ordinary subjects into puzzles that sparked curiosity. Even the most reluctant learner left with a sense of accomplishment.

**B. The Mentor Who Listened**  
Beyond the curriculum, Evelyn taught us how to listen. I remember a sophomore, Alex, who was battling self‑doubt after a poor math test. Instead of focusing on the grade, Mrs. Carter spent an hour after school walking him through problem‑solving strategies—while gently reminding him that a single test does not define his worth. Alex went on to ace his AP calculus final and later pursued an engineering degree. The ripple effect of that one conversation has been felt far beyond that day.

**C. The Champion of Community**  
Evelyn didn’t limit her influence to the four walls of her classroom. She spearheaded the school’s annual “Literature & Lanterns” night, organized the science fair mentorship program, and rallied volunteers for the neighborhood food drive. Under her leadership, the school garden blossomed into a living laboratory for biology, nutrition, and even interdisciplinary art projects. In short, she taught us that education is a community effort.

---

### 3. What She Has Learned From Us  

As much as we have learned from Evelyn, she has also taught us a vital lesson about humility and the joy of continuous growth. She once told a gathering of new teachers, “Even after 30 years, I still feel the awe of the first ‘aha!’ moment. It reminds me that learning is a two‑way street.” That openness to learning, even after three decades, has inspired countless colleagues to stay curious, stay flexible, and stay kind.

---

### 4. A Few Voices From the Hallways  

*“Mrs. Carter, you made me believe I could write my own story.”* – Maya, former 8th‑grade student, now a published author.  

*“Your patience turned my fear of numbers into a love for patterns. I’m now a data analyst, and I credit you for that.”* – Jordan, alumnus, tech startup founder.  

*“Evelyn, you taught our department that collaboration isn’t a buzzword; it’s a lifeline.”* – Mr. Patel, fellow teacher and longtime friend.  

These snippets capture just a fraction of the impact she has had. If we could list every life she’s touched, the length of this speech would rival the novels that line her bookshelf.

---

### 5. Looking Forward  

Retirement, as we know, isn’t an ending—it’s a transition. Evelyn, we have no doubt that you’ll approach this new chapter with the same enthusiasm you brought to lesson planning. Whether you finally get to finish that novel you’ve been drafting, spend sunrise mornings in the garden you helped create, or volunteer at the local library, we know you’ll continue to inspire, to teach, and to love.

We also expect a few grand gestures: perhaps a weekly “Evelyn’s Book Club” at the community center, or a mentorship program that bears your name. The school is already drafting a “Evelyn Carter Scholarship” for students who embody the curiosity and compassion you championed.

---

### 6. A Heartfelt Thank You  

On behalf of the entire school community—students, parents, staff, and administrators—thank you, Evelyn, for:

* Your unwavering dedication, day after day, year after year.  
* Your boundless compassion, which turned obstacles into stepping stones.  
* Your relentless optimism, which reminded us that every challenge is an opportunity to learn.  

Your legacy is etched in the walls of this school, in the pages of countless journals, and most importantly, in the hearts of the people whose lives you have forever changed.

---

### 7. Closing  

As we celebrate this moment, let us raise our glasses—not just to a career well‑spent, but to a future bright with possibility. May your retirement be filled with quiet mornings, adventurous afternoons, and endless evenings of storytelling—just as you have given us for the past thirty years.

*Mrs. Carter, thank you for teaching us not just how to read the world, but how to love it.*

Cheers to you, and happy retirement!

---

**Speech Title: “The Super‑Power of Kindness”**  
*Delivered at the Elementary School Assembly*  

---

**[Begin with a Warm Welcome]**  
Good morning, Bright Stars of [School Name]!  
I’m so happy to be here with you today. Look around—see all those smiling faces? That’s exactly what kindness helps create: a room full of brightness, friendship, and good feelings.

---

### 1. What Is Kindness?

*“Kindness is doing something nice for someone else—no matter how small—just because you care.”*  

- **It’s a smile** you give to a friend who’s feeling shy.  
- **It’s a helping hand** when a classmate drops their books.  
- **It’s a kind word** when someone makes a mistake.  

Kindness isn’t a big, fancy thing; it’s a collection of tiny actions that add up to something huge.

---

### 2. Why Kindness Matters—Three Super‑Power Reasons

1. **Kindness Makes You Feel Great**  
   When you do something kind, your brain releases a “feel‑good” chemical called *dopamine*. It’s the same happy buzz you get when you eat your favorite ice‑cream! So the more kind you are, the happier you become.

2. **Kindness Builds Strong Friendships**  
   Think of a friendship like a bridge. Every kind act is a plank that makes the bridge longer and stronger. When you help a classmate, they’re more likely to help you later—creating a circle of support that never breaks.

3. **Kindness Makes the Whole School Shine**  
   One kind word can turn a gloomy hallway into a place where everyone wants to be. When we all practice kindness, our school becomes a place where learning feels safe, fun, and exciting.

---

### 3. A Little Story—The Ripple Effect

Let me tell you a quick story about a girl named Maya.

One day, Maya noticed a new student, Carlos, sitting alone during lunch. She walked over, offered him her sandwich, and asked, “Do you want to play tag after school?”

```python
def is_leap_year(year: int) -> bool:
    """
    Return True if *year* is a leap year, otherwise False.

    Gregorian calendar rules
    ------------------------
    * Every year divisible by 4 is a leap year…
    * …except those that are also divisible by 100,
    * unless the year is divisible by 400.

    Parameters
    ----------
    year: int
        The year to test.  Works for any integer (positive, zero, or negative).

    Returns
    -------
    bool
        True for leap years, False otherwise.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> is_leap_year(2000)
    True
    >>> is_leap_year(1900)
    False
    >>> is_leap_year(2024)
    True
    """
    # First check the 400‑year rule (the most specific)
    if year % 400 == 0:
        return True
    # Then the 100‑year rule (exclude these)
    if year % 100 == 0:
        return False
    # Finally the 4‑year rule (include these)
    return year % 4 == 0


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Simple sanity‑check tests (they will raise an AssertionError if anything is wrong)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    assert is_leap_year(2000) == True   # divisible by 400
    assert is_leap_year(1900) == False  # divisible by 100 but not 400
    assert is_leap_year(2024) == True   # regular 4‑year leap
    assert is_leap_year(2023) == False  # not a leap year
    assert is_leap_year(0) == True      # year 0 is a multiple of 400
    print("All tests passed!")
```

### How it works
1. **`year % 400 == 0`** – If the year is divisible by 400, it is definitely a leap year.
2. **`year % 100 == 0`** – If the year is divisible by 100 *but not* by 400, it is **not** a leap year.
3. **`year % 4 == 0`** – For the remaining years, being divisible by 4 makes it a leap year; otherwise it isn’t.

```python
def count_vowels(s: str) -> int:
    """
    Return the number of vowels (a, e, i, o, u) in *s*.
    The check is case‑insensitive.

    >>> count_vowels('Hello')
    2

    0

    # A set gives O(1) membership checks and works with any iterable string.
    vowels = set('aeiouAEIOU')
```

```python
def second_largest(nums):
    """
    Return the second‑largest *distinct* number in ``nums``.

    Parameters
    ----------
    nums : iterable of numbers
        The collection to search.  It must contain at least two *different*
        values; otherwise a ``ValueError`` is raised.

    Returns
    -------
    number
        The second‑largest distinct value.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> second_largest([3, 1, 4, 1, 5])
    4
    >>> second_largest([10, 10, 9])
    9
    >>> second_largest([-2, -1])
    -2
    >>> second_largest([7, 7, 7, 7, 5])
    5
    """
    # 1️⃣  Remove duplicates – we only care about distinct values.
    distinct = set(nums)

    # 2️⃣  We need at least two different numbers.
    if len(distinct) < 2:
        raise ValueError("need at least two distinct numbers")

    # 3️⃣  Find the largest and second‑largest in one pass.
    #      Using ``float('-inf')`` works for any comparable numeric type.
    first = second = float("-inf")
    for n in distinct:
        if n > first:
            second = first   # previous largest becomes second largest
            first = n
        elif n > second:
            second = n

    return second
```

### How it works
1. **`set(nums)`** knocks out duplicates, so repeated values (e.g., the two 10’s in the second test) don’t affect the result.
2. We guard against the situation where the input contains fewer than two distinct numbers – a `ValueError` makes the failure explicit.

**Solution Overview**

A Roman numeral is read from left to right.  
Normally each symbol adds its value, but when a *smaller* symbol appears **before** a *larger* one it means “subtract the smaller value”.  
The classic set of symbols is  

| Symbol | Value |
|--------|-------|
| I      | 1     |
| V      | 5     |
| X      | 10    |
| L      | 50    |
| C      | 100   |
| D      | 500   |
| M      | 1000  |

The conversion algorithm is therefore:

1. Scan the string from left to right.
2. Look at the current symbol and the next symbol (if any).
3. If the current value is **smaller** than the next value → **subtract** it from the total.
4. Otherwise → **add** it to the total.
5. Continue until the end of the string.

The algorithm runs in linear time **O(n)** and uses only constant extra space.

---

### Code

```python
def roman_to_int(s: str) -> int:
    """
    Convert a Roman numeral string to its integer value.

    Parameters
    ----------
    s : str
        A non‑empty string containing only the characters
        I, V, X, L, C, D, M (uppercase).

    Returns
    -------
    int
        The integer representation of the Roman numeral.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> roman_to_int('III')
    3
    >>> roman_to_int('IX')
    9
    >>> roman_to_int('MCMXCIV')
    1994
    """
    # Mapping from Roman symbol to its integer value
    value = {
        'I': 1,
        'V': 5,
        'X': 10,
        'L': 50,
        'C': 100,
        'D': 500,
        'M': 1000,
    }

    total = 0
    i = 0
    n = len(s)

    while i < n:
        cur_val = value[s[i]]

        # Peek at the next character, if any
        if i + 1 < n:
            next_val = value[s[i + 1]]
            # Subtractive pair (e.g., IV, IX, XL, ...)
            if cur_val < next_val:
                total += next_val - cur_val
                i += 2          # skip both characters
                continue

        # Normal additive case
        total += cur_val
        i += 1

    return total
```

---

### Explanation of the Core Loop  

```python
while i < n:
    cur_val = value[s[i]]
    if i + 1 < n:
        next_val = value[s[i + 1]]
        if cur_val < next_val:          # e.g., I before V => 4
            total += next_val - cur_val
            i += 2                      # consume both symbols
            continue
    total += cur_val
    i += 1
```

* `cur_val < next_val` detects the subtractive pattern.
* When it occurs we add the **difference** (`next_val - cur_val`) and skip the next character because it has already been accounted for.
* Otherwise we simply add the current symbol’s value.

---

```python
    ------

        elif isinstance(item, list):

        else:
            # You could choose to silently ignore unknown types, but raising
```

```python
def run_length_encode(s: str) -> str:
    """
    Return the run‑length encoding of *s*.
    Each character is followed by the number of consecutive occurrences.
    
    Examples
    --------
    >>> run_length_encode('aaab')
    'a3b1'
    >>> run_length_encode('')
    ''
    >>> run_length_encode('abc')
    'a1b1c1'
    """
    if not s:                     # empty input → empty output
        return ""

    encoded_parts = []            # collect pieces as we go
    prev_char = s[0]              # first character of the current run
    count = 1                     # how many times we've seen it so far

    # Walk through the rest of the string
    for ch in s[1:]:
        if ch == prev_char:       # same run, just increase the counter
            count += 1
        else:                     # run finished – emit it
            encoded_parts.append(f"{prev_char}{count}")
            prev_char = ch        # start a new run
            count = 1

    # Emit the final run (the loop stops before writing it)
    encoded_parts.append(f"{prev_char}{count}")

    # Join the list into the final string
    return "".join(encoded_parts)
```

```python
def gcd(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """
    Return the greatest common divisor of a and b using the Euclidean algorithm.

    Parameters
    ----------
    a, b : int
        Non‑negative integers.  If both are zero the result is defined as 0
        (the mathematical convention for “gcd(0,0)”), otherwise the function
        returns the largest integer that divides both numbers.

    Returns
    -------
    int
        The greatest common divisor of a and b.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> gcd(12, 18)
    6
    >>> gcd(7, 0)
    7
    >>> gcd(17, 5)
    1
    """
    # Guard against negative inputs – the spec says non‑negative, so we raise
    # a clear error if the caller violates that contract.
    if a < 0 or b < 0:
        raise ValueError("gcd is defined only for non‑negative integers")

    # Euclidean algorithm: repeatedly replace the larger number by the
    # remainder of the division until the remainder becomes 0.
    while b:
        a, b = b, a % b
    return a   # when b == 0, a holds the GCD
```

### How it works
1. **Input validation** – If either argument is negative we raise a `ValueError` to make misuse obvious.
2. **Main loop** – `while b:` runs as long as the second number (`b`) is not zero.  
   In each iteration we set `a` to the current `b` and `b` to `a % b` (the remainder).  
   This is the classic Euclidean algorithm, which converges to the greatest
   common divisor in at most `O(log min(a, b))` steps.
3. **Result** – When `b` becomes `0`, `a` is the greatest common divisor.  
   The special case `gcd(x, 0)` automatically returns `x`, satisfying the example
   `gcd(7, 0) == 7`. If both inputs are `0`, the loop never executes and the
   function returns `0`, which is a conventional (though not universally
   accepted) definition for `gcd(0, 0)`.

```python
def median(nums):
    """
    Return the statistical median of a non‑empty list (or any iterable) of numbers.

    The median is the value separating the higher half from the lower half of a data
    sample.  For an odd number of items it is the middle element after sorting.
    For an even number of items it is the arithmetic mean of the two middle elements.

    Parameters
    ----------
    nums : Sequence[Number]
        A non‑empty iterable of comparable numeric values.

    Returns
    -------
    float or int
        The median of the input values.  The return type matches the type of the
        intermediate arithmetic (e.g. a float if the average of two ints is not integral).

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If *nums* is empty.

    Example
    -------
    >>> median([3, 1, 2])
    2
    >>> median([4, 1, 3, 2])
    2.5
    >>> median([5])
    5
    """
    # Convert to a list so we can sort it and also support any iterable input
    data = list(nums)

    if not data:
        raise ValueError("median() arg is an empty sequence")

    data.sort()                      # O(n log n) – the standard way for median
    n = len(data)
    mid = n // 2

    if n % 2:                        # odd length → single middle element
        return data[mid]
    else:                            # even length → average of the two middles
        # Using (a + b) / 2 works for ints, floats, Decimal, Fraction, etc.
        return (data[mid - 1] + data[mid]) / 2
```
